questions.question: Describe the four phases of the business cycle with the signature conditions of each, and state the working definition of a recession.
questions.expected_answer: Upswing: output, hiring, incomes and spending all rising, each round feeding the next — injections outrunning leakages. Peak: the upper turning point — activity at full stretch, factories near capacity, jobs plentiful, but prices straining upward and scarce skills at a premium. Downswing: output sliding, retrenchments spreading, incomes and spending shrinking — the contracting spiral; deep and prolonged, it becomes a recession. Trough: the lower turning point — activity weakest, but recovery ingredients gathering: low costs, cheaper borrowing, replacement demand accumulating. The cycle repeats without a timetable. Recession, verbatim: two consecutive quarters of declining real GDP.

questions.question: Classify economic indicators by timing with an example and reason for each, and explain the Reserve Bank's role.
questions.expected_answer: Leading indicators turn before the economy — building plans approved, new vehicle orders, share prices, confidence surveys — because they record today's decisions about tomorrow's activity: they warn. Coincident indicators move with the cycle — current production, retail sales, this month's employment: they confirm the present. Lagging indicators turn after — unemployment (firms retrench late and rehire late), inventories, outstanding credit: they certify the past. The Reserve Bank compiles composite leading, coincident and lagging indicators — bundles of many series — and officially dates the national cycle, announcing after the fact when upswings and downswings began and ended.

questions.question: Name the four movements inside a time series, separate exogenous from endogenous causes with examples, and describe who carries the downswing's heaviest costs.
questions.expected_answer: Four movements: the trend (decades-long direction), the cyclical wave (the business cycle), the seasonal pattern (calendar-driven, e.g. December retail — removed by seasonal adjustment so the cycle shows), and irregular one-off shocks (a flood, a strike). Exogenous causes come from outside the system: drought, war, pandemics, world commodity price swings hitting our mining towns. Endogenous causes grow inside it: self-feeding waves of optimism and pessimism, and credit expanding in booms then tightening sharply. Real cycles usually mix both. The downswing lands unequally: the last hired and least skilled are retrenched first, townships feel it before office parks, government loses revenue exactly as need rises, and postponed investment weakens the next upswing.
